claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and high-speed DIC can capture evolving local strain fields and microstructural dynamics during tensile and fracture testing.
Simultaneous diffraction and DIC measurements can determine the time-dependent evolution of local strains and phase distributions.
The relevant structural mediator comprises the spatial distribution and evolution of grain boundaries, sub-grain features, and interphase interfaces in HfNbTiVAl10.
Real-time local strain data reflect the alloy's heterogeneous microstructure.
Real-time local strain data can be used to train and continuously update a machine-learning surrogate model.
Synthetic data from validated physics-based simulations and fundamental mechanical constraints can augment the surrogate model.
A surrogate model can map material descriptors to macroscopic mechanical responses.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict yield strength.
The proposed surrogate can predict Young's modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can predict fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Surrogate modeling can be computationally easier or more efficient than strict physics-based calculations.
The proposed model will reduce simulation time by roughly 50% relative to conventional simulation methods.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness more accurately than conventional simulations.
The accuracy of a surrogate model strongly depends on the dataset, selected features, and machine-learning algorithm.
Poor-quality in situ data can limit the proposed model's performance.
Microstructural evolution outside the training distribution, particularly at extreme strains, can limit model generalizability.
Consistent prediction errors greater than 10% across multiple independent samples and test conditions are declared to falsify the hypothesis.
